narrative:
The model estimated a 66.3% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because that risk estimate exceeded the threshold used for admission, your law-school application was rejected. This is not a finding that you cannot pass; it means your profile, as summarized by the model, looked closer to students who failed than to those who passed.

The single strongest factor was your third-year class-rank decile: you are in decile 1, while accepted students average near 5.8. This very low relative standing pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. The second most influential factor was your first-year class-rank decile: decile 5 versus an accepted average of 6. It modestly pushed the prediction toward passing. Third was your LSAT score of 34, below the accepted average of 37.18; despite being below average, it contributed modestly toward passing rather than failure.

To improve future applications, focus on the clearest risk signal: raise your academic standing in advanced coursework and provide context for the low third-year rank if there were extenuating circumstances. Consider retaking the LSAT, strengthening your GPA through additional coursework, and applying to programs that review applicants holistically. A reconsideration request could include a concise explanation of your trajectory and concrete evidence of improved preparation for bar-level study.
